edge.title: The job that charges you
edge.setup: An offer letter arrives — good company, better package than you expected, for a role you half-remember applying to. HR is responsive and warm. There's a refundable registration, or a laptop deposit, or a background-verification fee. ₹4,000 to ₹25,000, payable today to confirm the seat.
edge.tell: Money flowing from employee to employer, in any form, at any stage.
move: Legitimate employers never charge you. Not for verification, not for equipment, not refundably.
Verify via the company's official domain and switchboard — never a number or email in the offer itself.
Check the offer's email domain character by character. @infosys-hr.com is not @infosys.com.
edge.why: The scam exploits the asymmetry of hope: a job changes your life, so a small fee feels like a rounding error against the upside. That asymmetry is also why victims stay silent, which is why these keep running.
edge.variants: Same shape: work-from-home data-entry kits, 'task' and review-earning schemes that start by paying you, visa-processing fees for offers abroad.

lens.name: Survivorship bias
lens.one_line: You only see the things that made it, so you learn the wrong lesson from them.
lens.detail: The classic case: WWII engineers wanted to armour the bullet holes on returning planes, until Abraham Wald pointed out those were the survivable hits — the armour belonged where returning planes had no holes, because planes hit there never came back. Every 'habits of successful people' list has the same flaw: the identically-behaving failures aren't available to interview.
elsewhere: Dropout-founder stories, drawn from the tiny surviving tail.
Fund performance tables that quietly exclude closed funds.
Old buildings seeming better built — the shoddy ones were demolished.
lens.test: Who is missing from this dataset because they didn't make it this far?
lens.today: TOI's #IamBengaluru series reports that complaints have turned into action for Jakkur Lake (Times of India). It is a good story, and it is the one that got told. The lakes and stretches where complaints went nowhere don't make headlines, so a handful of fixes can make civic action look more reliable than it is; judge a process by how often it works for ordinary complaints, not by the ones that were reported.

moved.what: Bengaluru's debate over protest venues continues: the government defends the right to protest while activists ask why they are 'caged' at Freedom Park, after a march by anti-SIR activists was blocked (Times of India).
moved.so_what: Expect police barricades and slow traffic around Freedom Park and the central city when a march is planned. Check for a protest before you head into that stretch and leave extra time.

moved.what: Booth-level officers in Karnataka are now focused on voter roll changes ahead of the October 22 deadline under the SIR exercise (Times of India).
moved.so_what: Check your name and address on the voter roll before October 22. If it is missing or wrong, you have little more than a week to act.

moved.what: Doddagubbi area has been given a new pincode (Times of India).
moved.so_what: If you live or receive deliveries there, update the pincode on your bank, Aadhaar, KYC and delivery apps so mail and courier items are not misrouted.

moved.what: A video from a Bengaluru pub shows an IAS officer abusing police who asked him for ID; he has been booked for assault (NDTV, The Hindu).
moved.so_what: Venues and police can ask for age or ID proof at pubs. Carry a government photo ID when you go out, and keep a digital copy as backup.

moved.what: Special trains from Keralam for the festival season have been announced (The Hindu).
moved.so_what: If you are travelling to or from Kerala this season, look at the special services now; festival-period seats go early.

carry_over.prompt: At a pump or restaurant your card leaves your sight, or the machine 'fails' and needs a second swipe. What is the tell?
carry_over.answer: Your card leaving your sight, or a swipe that mysteriously needs doing twice.
